records.name_note: Sources split in structure but converge in usage. NC State's Common Name(s) field for Aronia melanocarpa is a two-entry alphabetized list, "Black Berried Aronia" then "Black Chokeberry," whose order matches the page-title parenthetical -- but NC State's own body prose does not follow that order: it calls the plant "Black chokeberry," never "Black Berried Aronia." Three other admissible dedicated single-species pages agree with the body prose, not the alphabetized list: Missouri Botanical Garden's Common Name field ("black chokeberry"), RHS's plant-profile subtitle/page title ("black chokeberry"), and University of Maryland Extension's page title ("Black Chokeberry"). "Black Chokeberry" is therefore used as common_name. Separately, NC State's page for the sibling species Aronia arbutifolia lists "Chokeberry" and "Red Chokeberry" as its two common names, and that page's prose calls the species "the red chokeberry." Unqualified "Chokeberry" is therefore a name NC State assigns to A. arbutifolia, not to A. melanocarpa, whose list carries only "Black Berried Aronia" and "Black Chokeberry" (its prose uses "Chokeberry" generically for the astringent berries).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS, UMD) states toxicity scoped to cats or dogs. NC State's page carries no Poison block and no Poisonous/Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags at all. RHS's 'Potentially harmful' note ('The berries are edible, but bitter raw, and this tree is usually grown as an ornamental plant rather than to provide a crop of fruit in the UK') concerns raw-fruit palatability for humans, not animal toxicity, so it does not support toxic_to_pets.

chill_damage_f is left null: the only admissible chilling figure found, University of Maryland Extension's Aronia program page citing roughly 1000 chill hours under a dual-temperature model, is a dormancy chilling requirement, not a stated damage-onset temperature, per the rule against treating a chill-hour/hardiness figure as an onset temperature.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field lists exactly two entries, "Buttonbush" and "Button Bush", whose order matches the page-title parenthetical "Cephalanthus occidentalis (Buttonbush, Button Bush)" and the body prose, which opens "Buttonbush is a deciduous, perennial shrub..." — this two-entry list is a lead, and "Buttonbush" is the name the body prose actually uses. RHS's plant-profile subtitle instead reads "button bush" (one word split, lower case), with a longer "Other common names" list behind it: button willow, globe-flowered bush, honeybells, little snowballs, swamp globeflower, white pond-dogwood — none of which are promoted to lead status on that page. Clemson HGIC's factsheet, a dedicated single-species page, also leads with "buttonbush" in its body but separately notes an additional alternate name, "honey-bells", tied to historical use by beekeepers, not presented as a lead. Given NC State's and Clemson's agreement and NC State's title/body consistency, "Buttonbush" is used as the catalog's common name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension carries a Poison block (heading "Poisonous to Humans") for Cephalanthus occidentalis: Poison Severity is "Low"; Poison Symptoms reads "The toxin is found in the bark. Ingestion of the bark can cause vomiting, convulsions and paralysis."; Poison Toxic Principle is "Cephalathin"; Causes Contact Dermatitis is "No"; Poison Part is "Bark". This is a human-scoped rating — no NC State field states an onset dose or route beyond "ingestion of the bark." Separately, NC State's Problems list tags the plant "Problem for Horses"; no "Problem for Cats" or "Problem for Dogs" tag is present on the page, so this source gives no cat/dog-specific toxicity claim. UF/IFAS's EDIS/Ask IFAS publication corroborates the same low-severity, bark-based toxicity in its own words: "this plant exhibits low toxic characteristics; bark contains Cephalothin; causes issues if ingested" — again without naming any animal. RHS gives a differently-scoped warning about the foliage rather than the bark, and names no specific animal either: "Foliage may cause severe discomfort if eaten. Wear gloves and wash hands after handling." No admissible source scopes any toxicity claim to cats or dogs specifically.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is left null: the only toxicity evidence found across admissible sources is human-scoped (NC State's Poison block, corroborated by UF/IFAS) or scoped to horses (NC State's 'Problem for Horses' tag) or unscoped (RHS's foliage handling warning names no animal). No admissible source names cats or dogs.

soil_drainage moisture_retentive is read from NC State's and Clemson HGIC's cultivation statements ('needs consistently moist to wet, rich soils'; 'requires ... in moist to wet soils'), both species-specific. This conflicts with RHS's own cultivation-section statement ('moist but well-drained, neutral to acid soil'), which is a UK ornamental-trade profile; given two North American extension sources' explicit, direct 'wet' cultivation language against RHS's single 'well-drained' reading, moisture_retentive was chosen and the RHS conflict is disclosed here rather than silently dropped.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists only the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band (no floor), and RHS's Soil field states 'neutral to acid' categorically without numeric bounds, so no closed numeric band exists across sources to derive a ceiling or floor from.

MoBot's plantfinder.mobot.org page could not be fetched (a TLS certificate error blocked retrieval), so its Common Name field/tooltip and Culture section were not inspected and are not represented in this record.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's "Poisonous to Humans:" block (human-scoped, medium severity) states: Poison Severity "Medium"; Poison Symptoms "Skin contact with the sap, or ingestion of the plant, can cause photosensitivity in some people. Common side-effects are gastointestinal disturbances, allergic reactions and fatigue."; Poison Toxic Principle "Unidentified, possibly a glycoside"; Causes Contact Dermatitis "Yes"; and the full Poison Part list is "Leaves, Sap/Juice." NC State's separate Edibility note adds a drug-interaction warning: "Ingesting St John's wort can reduce the effectiveness of some prescription medicines." RHS's "Potentially harmful" field scopes its warning differently -- to the fruit only, not the leaves/sap: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers." RHS names "Pets" only as an unscoped generic category, not cats or dogs specifically, and no admissible source names cats or dogs by name, so toxic_to_pets is left null. Note the scope disagreement: NC State's poison-part list (leaves, sap/juice, by contact or ingestion) is broader than RHS's fruit-only framing.
